query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment that increases the thickness and continuity of the surface oxide film on the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating leads to improved overall wear resistance and reduced microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard-processed FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating as-deposited on a conventional metal substrate, featuring its typical microstructure, residual stresses, and adhesion characteristics with a naturally formed, less controlled oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a thermal oxidation pretreatment by subjecting the coating to a controlled temperature (e.g., 600–800°C) for a specified duration to deliberately increase the oxide film thickness and improve its continuity and adhesion.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (approximately 600–800°C) where thermally activated phenomena such as oxidation are significant during frictional contact.
generation.structural_mediator: The deliberately thickened and continuous surface oxide layer (likely with a spinel-type composition), which acts as a diffusion barrier and mechanical support.
generation.mechanism: A well-developed oxide film will distribute the applied load more uniformly and act as a protective barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding. This limits friction-induced plastic deformation and subsurface damage, thereby reducing the overall wear rate. The improved oxide scale quality should also inhibit the initiation of microcracks and suppress mechanisms that lead to premature wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (as-deposited) coating, the thermally oxidized coating will exhibit a measurable decrease in wear track depth and a reduction in microscopic signs of plastic deformation (e.g., fewer or smaller plastic zones, cracks, or deformation bands) when slid under high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with its naturally formed, uncontrolled oxide layer.
generation.boundary: These effects are anticipated within the high-temperature sliding regime (600–800°C) where thermal oxidation is active. Other regimes (e.g., room temperature) may not exhibit the same mechanistic benefits.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal oxide film thickness, composition, and microstructural characteristics that yield the best wear performance are not fully known. Variations in coating microstructural features and local oxidation kinetics may also influence the extent of the benefit.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coated samples on identical substrates: one set using the standard deposition process (baseline) and another set subjected to a controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment (600–800°C for a fixed duration). Conduct sliding wear tests at a high temperature (within the 600–800°C range) under identical load and sliding speed conditions. Analyze both the macroscopic wear track and the microscopic deformation (using techniques such as SEM and TEM) in the subsurface regions.
measurements: Wear track depth and width (quantified by profilometry)
Microstructural characterization of deformation zones (via SEM/TEM)
Oxide film thickness and continuity (using cross-sectional microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in wear resistance (i.e., similar or increased wear track dimensions, friction levels, and subsurface deformation features) compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis—that controlled thermal oxidation improves wear resistance by modifying microscopic deformation mechanisms—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

chosen.lever: thermal oxidation pretreatment to control the oxide film characteristics on the FeNiCrCoCu coating
chosen.technique: high-temperature sliding tribometry followed by detailed microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and XRD)
chosen.conditions: 600–800°C sliding tests in an ambient or controlled atmosphere that mimics the high-temperature operating regime
chosen.why: This move directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that a protective, nanocrystalline oxide layer governs both wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding. By imposing a controlled change (i.e. introducing a pre-determined oxide thickness via thermal oxidation) relative to the baseline as-deposited coating, the study can predict directional changes – namely, a thicker, well-adherent oxide layer should reduce wear and limit microscopic deformation. The approach leverages standard experimental techniques in materials science and addresses the open question by filling the niche with a testable, controlled variable experiment.

frame.system: A FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate. The baseline state is a standard‐processed coating with its typical microstructure, residual stresses, and adhesion characteristics as deposited onto the substrate.
frame.goal: To identify and validate a mechanistic hypothesis that links controlled microstructural or compositional changes in the coating to directional improvements (or degradations) in wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior under high-temperature sliding.
frame.limitation: An incomplete understanding exists regarding the dominant mechanisms controlling wear and deformation in these complex HEA coatings, especially at high operating temperatures. Specifically, it is unclear how thermally activated phenomena (e.g., phase transformations, grain boundary behavior, oxidation) influence friction and wear at the micro level.
constraints: Define a single, testable change relative to a baseline coating condition (e.g., a controlled increase in nano- or microstructural refinement or a shift in surface chemistry)
Predict corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation (i.e., either improvements or degradations)
The hypothesis must be applicable in a high-temperature sliding regime
It requires supporting evidence from prior studies and a clearly defined outcome that would falsify the hypothesis
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding conditions (for instance, in the range where thermally activated effects become significant; typically a few hundred degrees Celsius, e.g., 500–700 °C, though the exact temperature range should map to the alloy’s operating conditions)
prior_attempts: Previous experiments on similar HEA coatings have examined phase stability or oxidation effects separately without conclusively linking these factors to friction-induced microscopic deformation.

Studies focusing on microstructural refinement or grain boundary engineering in related alloys have noted changes in wear behavior but lacked a unified mechanistic explanation that integrates both wear resistance and deformation modes under elevated temperatures.

decision.trend: Early studies on high‐entropy alloy coatings under high-temperature conditions have largely probed how thermally induced phase changes and surface oxide formation influence wear. In PMC7515071, experimental wear tests on AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 at elevated temperatures showed that the formation of a protective oxide (spinel phase) correlates with improved wear resistance; meanwhile, PMC9026100 demonstrated that refining the microstructure through friction processing enhanced oxidation kinetics and shifted the oxide scale from nonprotective to protective. In sequence, researchers moved from characterizing basic microstructural responses (e.g., dynamic recrystallization or grain refinement) to linking the emergence of oxide films with directional wear performance. However, while the presence of oxide scales is repeatedly observed, the precise mechanistic link—namely, how a controlled change in the oxide layer (its thickness or composition) governs both macroscopic wear and microscopic deformation—is still not fully understood.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved issue is the direct mechanistic connection between a deliberately modified surface oxide layer (in terms of its thickness and quality) and its effect on microscopic deformation modes and overall wear resistance during high-temperature sliding in FeNiCrCoCu coatings. Specifically, it remains unclear how controlled thermal oxidation of the coating affects friction-induced subsurface deformation, and what oxide scale metrics (e.g., thickness, continuity, adhesion) directly modulate wear behavior under sliding at high temperatures.
decision.lever: thermal oxidation pretreatment to systematically modify the surface oxide film thickness
decision.why: Based on the experimental trends, previous studies have shown that naturally formed oxide films at elevated temperatures can enhance wear resistance. Applying a controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment on the baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating directly addresses the gap by allowing researchers to vary the oxide film’s thickness and quality. This lever—achievable by adjusting treatment time and temperature within the 600–800°C regime—provides a single, testable modification that can be clearly correlated with directional changes in wear and microscopic deformation. It occupies the open‐question niche by directly linking surface chemistry modification to mechanical performance under high-temperature sliding.
